Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Dmitri Holbrook is a 55-year-old single man of Eastern European descent who works as a counselor at a community mental health center in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, seeking help approximately fourteen months after surviving a gas explosion and fire that tore through the apartment building where he lived.

The event itself unfolded on an ordinary Tuesday evening. Dmitri had returned home from a late shift, heated something on the stove, and was moving through his hallway when a pressure wave knocked him off his feet. A gas main had ruptured in the unit below his, and the resulting explosion ignited a fire that spread rapidly through the lower floors. He remembers the heat arriving before the sound fully registered, and then — most vividly — the smell: a dense, acrid mixture of burning insulation, scorched wood, and something chemical and sweet underneath it all. He made it out through a stairwell that was already filling with smoke, pressing his sleeve to his face, and stood on the street watching the building burn while his ears rang and his legs refused to stop shaking. Two residents on the floor below him did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Dmitri moved into a short-term rental and told himself he was managing. He was not. The memory of that night did not come to him as a coherent story he could sit with; instead it arrived sideways — as a wave of dread with no accompanying image, a visceral flooding of fear whose source felt both undeniable and strangely unlocatable. More disorienting still was the quality of the memory when it did surface with any clarity: it felt, he told his intake clinician, as though it had happened to someone else, as though he were reading a case file about a man he did not quite recognise. He had come to believe this disconnection meant something was fundamentally wrong with him, that his mind was beginning to come apart in ways he could not name. He began watching his own thoughts with a vigilance he had previously reserved for clients in crisis — scanning for signs that he was losing his grip on reality, cataloguing each intrusion, each moment of blankness, each unfamiliar emotional surge as potential evidence of deterioration.

The smell triggers were among the earliest and most reliable. A neighbor burning leaves two blocks away, a colleague microwaving something in the break room, the faint trace of smoke from a passing truck — any of these could stop Dmitri mid-sentence and flood him with the same physical alarm his body had mounted on the night of the fire. He had come to regard his own physiology as something unreliable, even treacherous; his heart rate and the tightness in his chest were, to him, his body refusing to accept information his mind already knew. He found himself scanning every new environment for exits, for the faint chemical trace of gas, for anything that might precede catastrophe. What frightened him most was not that danger was present but that he could no longer trust himself to distinguish between when it was and when it was not.

At work, the trouble became concrete and consequential. Dmitri's office shares a building with a vocational training program, and when one of the workshop sessions involves any kind of heat tool — a soldering iron, a heat gun — the faint smell drifts into the hallway. On three separate occasions he had abruptly ended sessions with clients, offering vague explanations, and once he had asked a colleague to cover the remainder of his afternoon without being able to say why. He had stopped attending the informal Friday lunches his team maintained as a collegial ritual, finding that the unpredictability of what someone might say or do — a lighter, a candle, an anecdote involving fire — made the social setting feel unnavigable. The friendships that had sustained him for years were growing thin through his absence, and he was aware of this, and found he could not change it.

What finally brought Dmitri to seek help was a session last month in which a client, in distress, threw a folder of papers across the room. The sudden motion of the object through the air activated something in Dmitri that he could not contain in the room; he had to excuse himself. He sat in the men's room for ten minutes, waiting for his hands to stop trembling. He is a counselor. He knows what this looks like from the outside. What he hopes, with considerable ambivalence, is that understanding it professionally will eventually mean something to the part of him that does not feel like his own.
